results.title: Together AI Cuts GPU Cluster Pricing in Half for Interruptible Workloads | Superpower Daily
results.author: Superpower Daily Editorial Desk
highlights:
# Together AI Cuts GPU Cluster Pricing in Half for Interruptible Workloads

The public preview gives checkpointed jobs a cheaper way to scale, while putting reliability work—and the risk of sudden capacity loss—on customers.

By Superpower Daily Editorial Desk Published Sep 10, 2026, 5:09 PM PDT 2 min read

Together AI Cuts GPU Cluster Pricing in Half for Interruptible Workloads

 Read transcript

Together AI is opening a public preview that cuts the price of certain GPU capacity in half. Its new preemptible option runs NVIDIA GPU nodes at 50% of the on-demand rate, using spare capacity for workloads that can tolerate interruption. The trade-off is straightforward: Together can reclaim those nodes when it needs the capacity elsewhere. Affected Kubernetes pods receive a termination signal and get up to five minutes to checkpoint—that is, save enough progress to resume later—and exit before the node disappears. Together says the rate is fixed, rather than changing like a spot-market price, and usage is measured roughly every one to two minutes, so short jobs are billed for approximately the time they actually run. This works inside a normal Together GPU Cluster, not as a separate cluster. Customers must keep at least one standard node, while preemptible nodes can be added to new or existing clusters. Together can refill the requested preemptible capacity as spare capacity returns, but that target is not a reservation: live allocation may fall below it, and there is no minimum node lifetime. The model fits experiments, evaluations, fine-tuning, distillation, batch inference, and other restartable work. It is a poor match for multi-day jobs without checkpoints or strict serving without fallback. Kubernetes is supported in every region for now; Slurm, more regions, and in-place conversion are planned. The key constraint is whether a team’s software can make a sudden GPU loss routine instead of disruptive.

...

Together AI is testing a fixed-price preemptible option for its GPU Clusters, letting customers run restartable workloads at 50% of on-demand rates on spare NVIDIA capacity. The savings come with uncertain availability: nodes can be reclaimed, workloads get up to five minutes to checkpoint and exit, and configured capacity targets are not reservations.

...

Together AI has opened a public preview of preemptible compute for its GPU Clusters, offering NVIDIA GPU nodes at a flat half of the on-demand price. The trade is direct: teams can cut costs for restartable work, but Together can reclaim that capacity when it needs it elsewhere.

The preview is available on Kubernetes clusters in all regions and can be added to new or existing Together GPU Clusters. Rather than creating a separate cluster, the discounted nodes join an existing one alongside standard nodes, which Together says are fulfilled synchronously and are never preempted.

...

Preemptible nodes draw from unused capacity on the same NVIDIA accelerated-computing infrastructure. They are billed sub-hourly, with usage measured about every one to two minutes, so a short-lived worker is charged for roughly the time it runs rather than a full hour.

...

Together says the rate is fixed at half the on-demand price rather than changing with a spot market. When capacity is reclaimed, workloads have up to five minutes to save progress and exit before the node is removed.

...

When Together reclaims a node, it marks the node unavailable, sends affected pods a termination signal and emits a Kubernetes event. The workload then has a drain period of up to five minutes to checkpoint—save enough state to resume later—and shut down before the node disappears.

Aven Cloud's on-demand GPU prices, adjusted continuously to supply and demand, set against the public on-demand list prices of the three largest public clouds — sourced, dated, and backed by a published price history, all on the same page.

Updated 2026-09-10 · 5 min read

Every row combines Aven Cloud's live on-demand catalogue price — adjusted continuously to supply and demand — with the public on-demand list price published by each of the three largest public clouds for a comparable GPU. Nothing here is a quote or an estimate: the Aven Cloud side is the exact price you'd pay to order that GPU as of 14 November 2026, 07:59 UTC, and the reference side is a documented, dated list price (see Methodology below).

Per-second billing, no egress fees, release anytime.

On-demand is Aven Cloud's current single-GPU rate, adjusted continuously to supply and demand; spot is the interruptible rate for the same GPU where one is listed, and it can move on every refresh. results.title: H100 Rental Prices Halve to $3.43/Hr in 2026
results.author: Dr. Elena Marchetti
highlights:
Renting an Nvidia H100 for an hour costs anywhere from $1.30 an hour to as much as $12.29 in October 2026 according to Coloprice, depending on who you ask and which cloud you

...

Pricing tracker Thunder Compute, in a blog post on H100 pricing dated September 1, 2026, lists on-demand H100 80GB rates spanning from $2.89 an hour on RunPod up to $10.98 an hour on Google Cloud’s a3-highgpu-8g instances. CloudZero’s own H100 cost breakdown, published in late August 2026, puts the low end at Vast.ai for as little as $1.49 an hour, though GPUFinder’s October 2026 listing of $1.29 an hour on Hyperbolic now sets the floor, while Rank.ai listed Azure H100 capacity at $6.98 to $12.29 per GPU-hour in October 2026, which stretches the spread at the top even wider. Between those two data points sits a real number that infrastructure teams have to budget against every quarter.

...

Three tiers have emerged in the market and they behave almost like separate products. Marketplace and community-cloud rates sit at the floor, where platforms like RunPod’s community tier and Vast.ai’s peer-to-peer listings undercut everyone else. Specialist clouds such as Lambda, Nebius, and Crusoe occupy the middle, offering more reliability and support without hyperscaler markup (Hyperstack was reported at $2.50 an hour for H100 on a rate checked October 31, 2026, and Modal at $3.9492 an hour on a rate checked October 26, 2026), though that tier is not static: Nebius reportedly increased its H100 price from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour effective October 1, 2026, a rise of about 16.9% that formed part of a rate-card increase of as much as 21%. Hyperscaler on-demand pricing from AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud sits at the top, often two to four times the marketplace floor for the exact same chip.

| Chip | Marketplace / community floor | Specialist cloud (mid-tier) | Hyperscaler on-demand |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 80GB | $1.49–$2.99/hr | $3.19–$4.59/hr | $6.88–$10.98/hr |
| H200 141GB | $3.59/hr (RunPod Community) | $4.31–$4.59/hr | $5.58–$6.35/hr |
| B200 | Limited public data | $5.89/hr (RunPod tier cited by Hackceleration) | $8.64/hr (normalized Flex estimate) |

...

The H200 carries 141GB of HBM3e memory versus the H100’s 80GB, and cloud providers price that memory bump directly into the rental rate. RunPod’s community-cloud listing for H200 141GB has held at roughly $3.59 an hour through most of 2026, according to multiple pricing aggregators including DeployBase and Flexprice, while RunPod’s secure-cloud tier for the same chip runs $4.39 to $4.59 an hour. Hivenet’s own pricing page, updated August 28, 2026, lists H200 SXM configurations as high as $4.31 an hour for cluster-grade deployments, and Nebius lists H200 at $5.40 per GPU-hour effective October 1, 2026.

...

Retail-style pricing trackers show a wider range. Lambda lists B200 at $6.69 per GPU-hour for an eight-GPU configuration, RunPod Secure Cloud at $7.99 and Hyperstack at $6.00, while Nebius reportedly charges $8.50 from October 1, 2026 (up from $7.15, an increase of approximately 18.9%), a provider-specific increase rather than a rate every B200 provider charges, CoreWeave’s eight-GPU HGX B200 instance works out to about $8.60 per GPU, and AWS sits at the top of the range at $14.24. A Nebius preemptible B200 listing was reported at $5.00 per GPU-hour in one region on October 29, 2026, though that figure is not directly comparable with on-demand pricing. Blackwell Ultra is priced publicly too: Nebius lists B300 at $9.50 from October 1, 2026, Verda at $8.20, Scaleway at $7.50 and Together AI at $9.99.

results.title: GPU Hour Pricing: A $3.44 Rate Cost $68.80 to Use | THE D*AI*LY BRIEF
results.author: Rajesh Beri
highlights:
Sixty-four B200s cost between $1.93M and $9.03M for a year depending only on how you buy them. But at the 5% GPU utilisation Cast AI measured across 23,000 production clusters, a committed $3.44/hr rate bills out at $68.80 per useful GPU-hour — and the break-even duty cycle is 48%.

By Rajesh Beri· September 8, 2026· 17 min read

You are about to spend a quarter negotiating 15% off a GPU hour, and lose 2,000% on the hour you never used.

Here is the verdict before the analysis. Buy on-demand from a neocloud until you can prove a duty cycle above roughly 50%, then commit — and never sign a commitment whose break-even utilisation is higher than the utilisation you have actually measured. For most enterprise AI teams that means Nebius or Together AI on the meter for the first two quarters, a 3-to-6-month committed rate after that, and spot reserved strictly for checkpointed training. Google Cloud's A4 is the loser on this table and it is not close: the highest list rate of the nine, and the only one you cannot buy on demand at all.

## What 64 B200s Cost for a Year, by How You Buy Them

Normalised to one workload for every row: 64 NVIDIA B200 GPUs — eight nodes of eight — held for twelve months. That is 560,640 GPU-hours at a 100% duty cycle. Same silicon, same node topology. The only variable is the purchasing instrument. All rates were read off each vendor's live pricing page, or a public price tracker where the vendor publishes none, on 8 September 2026.

| Purchase mode | Product | $/GPU-hr | 12 months, 64 GPUs | Break-even duty | Can you exit? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Committed term | CoreWeave Reserved (up to 60% off) | ~$3.44 | $1.93M | 40% | Contract term |
| Preemptible | Together AI preemptible B200 | $4.09 | $2.29M | Tolerates 50% waste | Instantly — against you |
| Reserved, 91–180d | Together AI Reserved Capacity | $6.79 | $3.81M | 83% | At term end |
| On-demand | Nebius HGX B200 | $7.15 | $4.01M | n/a | Hourly |
| On-demand | CoreWeave HGX B200 | $8.60 | $4.82M | n/a | Hourly |
| Reserved cluster | Lambda 1-Click Cluster, 64 GPU | $9.36 | $5.25M | n/a | 2-week minimum |
| Reserved block | AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks, p6-b200 | $12.36 | $6.93M | 87% | No — non-cancellable |
| On-demand | AWS p6-b200.48xlarge | $14.24 | $7.98M | n/a | Hourly |
| Reservation-only | Google Cloud A4 (a4-highgpu-8g) | $16.11 | $9.03M | n/a | No on-demand option |

Sources, in order. CoreWeave lists HGX B200 at $68.80 per 8-GPU node — $8.60 per GPU — and advertises Reserved Compute Capacity at "up to 60% discounts over On-Demand prices for committed usage"; $3.44 is that ceiling applied, and it is the only estimated figure in the table. Together AI publishes the rare public ladder: $8.19 on-demand, $7.99 at 7–30 days, $7.79 at 31–90 days, $6.79 at 91–180 days, and $4.09 preemptible. Nebius lists HGX B200 at $7.15 on-demand and $3.95 preemptible. Lambda charges $9.86 per GPU at 16 GPUs, $9.36 at 64 and $8.87 at 256+. AWS prices Capacity Blocks for p6-b200 at $12.355 per accelerator-hour, against an on-demand p6-b200.48xlarge rate of $113.933 per instance-hour, which is $14.242 per GPU. Google's a4-highgpu-8g carries eight B200s at roughly $16.11 per GPU-hour — an on-demand-equivalent rate, since Google publishes no on-demand price for the machine type.

...

The published discounts are real and large: Together AI's preemptible B200 is $4.09 against $8.19 on-demand (50%), Nebius's is $3.95 against $7.15 (45%), CoreWeave's is $34.11 per node against $68.80 (50%), and AWS spot on p6-b200.48xlarge was $42.063 per instance-hour against $113.933 on-demand (63%). The useful way to read a spot discount is as a waste budget: at 50% off you can lose half of every job to preemption and still be level with on-demand.

results.title: What is a neocloud, and how does it price GPUs?
results.author: The Hardware Desk
highlights:
A neocloud rents Nvidia GPUs and nothing else; CoreWeave's HGX H100 node lists at $6.16 per GPU-hour on-demand, up to 60% cheaper on a multi-year commit. 

 Published 2026.09.10 · The Hardware Desk 

S SemiAnalysis — AI Neocloud Playbook and Anatomy↗ newsletter.semianalysis.com C CoreWeave, Inc. — Q1 2026 Earnings Press Release (SEC filing)↗ sec.gov C CoreWeave — GPU Cloud Pricing↗ coreweave.com L Lambda — GPU Cloud Pricing↗ lambda.ai O Ornn Data — Compute Price Index↗ data.ornn.com

A neocloud is a cloud provider, such as CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius or Crusoe, built entirely around renting Nvidia GPUs rather than general-purpose compute; it prices capacity on two tiers, a high hourly on-demand rate for flexibility and a discounted multi-year committed rate, with the gap (CoreWeave's HGX H100 runs $6.16 per GPU-hour on-demand versus up to 60% less reserved) funding the debt used to buy the GPUs in the first place.

...

- ▸ A neocloud is a cloud provider built entirely around GPU rental, a term SemiAnalysis coined on 3 October 2024 to separate CoreWeave-style specialists from AWS, Azure and GCP.
- ▸ CoreWeave's on-demand HGX H100 node lists at $49.24/hour for 8 GPUs, or $6.16 per GPU-hour, versus up to 60% off for a multi-year committed contract.
- ▸ The blended market rate for an H100 SXM was $2.68 per GPU-hour on 2026-08-26 per Ornn Data's index, well under any single neocloud's posted on-demand sticker.
- ▸ CoreWeave's revenue backlog reached $99.4 billion as of 2026-03-31, the contracted demand that lets it borrow against unbuilt data centers to keep expanding.
- ▸ Neocloud spot pricing swings hard: CoreWeave's HGX H100 spot rate is $19.71/hour, 60% below on-demand, because unsold capacity is a sunk cost the moment the GPU is idle.

 Every Nvidia model Artificial Analysis scores, best first — Nemotron 3.5 Super VL leads the lineup. Charted: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL · Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B · Nemotron 3.5 Lightning · NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano 4B Data: Artificial Analysis — independent benchmarks, not vendor-reported · measured 2026-11-14 06:10 UTC 

A neocloud is a cloud provider built entirely around renting Nvidia GPUs, nothing else, and it prices that capacity on two tiers: a high hourly rate for anyone who shows up without a commitment, and a discount of up to 60% for anyone willing to sign a multi-year contract. CoreWeave’s on-demand HGX H100 node runs $49.24 an hour for eight GPUs, or $6.16 per GPU-hour, a rate you can read straight off its public pricing page. The skill this post is really teaching is how to read that gap between on-demand and reserved pricing and understand why it exists, because it tells you exactly what a neocloud is betting on and what happens to your bill if that bet goes wrong.

...

A neocloud is a specialist cloud provider, CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius and Crusoe are the four SemiAnalysis classified as “neocloud giants” in its October 2024 taxonomy, that sells GPU rental almost exclusively instead of the broad service catalog a hyperscaler like AWS or Azure bundles. Pricing runs on two tracks: an on-demand hourly rate priced for flexibility and idle-capacity risk, and a reserved or committed rate discounted against multi-year contracts, up to 60% off on CoreWeave’s own pricing page. A blended market rate sits below either extreme: Ornn Data’s H100 SXM index settled at $2.68 per GPU-hour on 2026-08-26, versus CoreWeave’s $6.16 on-demand sticker for the same chip. The reserved discount exists because a signed, multi-year contract is exactly what lets a neocloud borrow money to buy the GPUs in the first place, so the price you’re quoted is really a reflection of how much certainty you’re giving the provider.

...

A neocloud’s business starts with debt, not with a data center. The provider needs tens of thousands of Nvidia GPUs, each one a five- or six-figure capital outlay before power and networking, and it typically can’t fund that from operating cash flow alone. So it signs a multi-year take-or-pay contract with a hyperscaler or an AI lab first, then uses that contract as collateral to borrow the money to buy the hardware. CoreWeave’s relationship with Microsoft is the clearest public example: the two companies have operated under a Master Service Agreement dating to February 2023, and that scale of committed demand is the kind of anchor a lender underwrites against. Once the GPUs are bought and racked inside a leased or purpose-built facility (What is a data center?), the neocloud has to sell every hour of capacity it can, because the GPUs depreciate and the debt service comes due whether or not anyone is renting that hour. Unlike a hyperscaler, which can shift idle GPU capacity onto dozens of other services (storage, databases, general compute), a neocloud has no such fallback: an unsold GPU-hour is just gone.

That single fact, an idle GPU costs money and an idle GPU earns nothing, explains the whole pricing structure. On-demand rates are set high because that customer is asking for maximum flexibility with zero commitment, so the provider prices in both the option value it’s giving up and the risk that the same hour goes unsold to someone else. Reserved or committed rates are set low because that customer is providing exactly what a lender wants to see: predictable, contracted cash flow over a multi-year term, the kind of backlog that let CoreWeave carry $99.4 billion in signed but not-yet-delivered revenue as of 2026-03-31. Spot pricing sits at the opposite extreme from on-demand: CoreWeave lists spot HGX H100 capacity at $19.71 an hour, 60% below its on-demand rate, because spot is explicitly the leftover capacity a provider would rather sell cheap than leave idle. The underlying Nvidia H100 silicon (What is a GPU?) doesn’t change between these tiers; only the certainty attached to the rental does.

## The numbers

The gap between on-demand and reserved pricing, and between one neocloud’s sticker price and the broader market, is the whole story. CoreWeave’s own pricing page lists three current Nvidia generations, each as an eight-GPU HGX node:

| GPU (8x HGX node) | On-demand, per node | On-demand, per GPU-hour | Spot, per GPU-hour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | $49.24/hr | $6.16 | $2.46 |
| H200 | $50.44/hr | $6.31 | $2.62 |
| B200 | $68.80/hr | $8.60 | $4.26 |

Lambda prices per GPU rather than per node: its H100 SXM runs $3.99 to $4.29 per GPU-hour on-demand and its B200 SXM6 runs $6.69 to $6.99, both lower than CoreWeave’s equivalent on-demand figures, which is consistent with Lambda competing on price within the same neocloud-giant tier. Against both of those sits Ornn Data’s blended H100 index, the same number that answers how much does it cost to rent an H100 per hour?, which settled at $2.68 per GPU-hour on 2026-08-26, below every on-demand figure above because the index averages across many providers and contract structures, including the deep reserved discounts that never show up on a public on-demand rate card. CoreWeave doesn’t publish what those reserved rates actually are by term length or volume, only that committed usage saves “up to 60% over on-demand prices,” so the number a given customer pays sits somewhere between that index average and the on-demand ceiling depending entirely on what they’re willing to sign. Underneath all of this, CoreWeave reported $2.078 billion in Q1 2026 revenue and a 56% adjusted EBITDA margin against that $99.4 billion backlog, evidence that the reserved side of the business, not the on-demand sticker, is what actually funds the buildout.

...

CoreWeave advertises up to 60% off on-demand pricing for committed usage, though it does not publish a public rate card by term length, GPU generation or volume; you get a specific number after a sales conversation.
